item.title: It’s April Fools Day! What does that actually mean? - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Mary Apel
item.description:
April Fools’ Day, celebrated on April 1st each year, has a history shrouded in folklore. While the exact origins of this playful day are unclear, there are several theories that attempt to explain its inception.

One popular theory traces the tradition back to the change from the Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar in the late 16th century when New Year’s Day moved from the end of March to January 1st. Those who continued to celebrate the New Year in April were labeled as fools and became the subjects of pranks and jokes.

Another theory links April Fools’ Day to ancient Roman and Celtic festivities that marked the arrival of spring with lighthearted pranks and mischievous behavior. Some even suggest a connection to the Roman festival of Hilaria, a day of laughter and jokes celebrated at the end of March.

The purpose of April Fools’ Day is to embrace lighthearted humor and playfulness, allowing people to engage in (hopefully harmless) pranks and jokes. It serves as a day to step away from the seriousness of everyday life and to share laughter with friends and family. The tradition of playing pranks on April 1st lets us spread a little joy and humor in a world that often needs a moment of levity.

item.title: "The Haven" helps incarcerated women find personal growth and recovery - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
The Mississippi Department of Corrections recognized the first graduating class of “The Haven,” a residential rehabilitation program developed within the Mississippi Correctional Institute for Women, during a recent ceremony honoring 23 incarcerated women who completed the program’s initial phase.

“The Haven” is a peer-developed initiative created by incarcerated women to support others working toward personal growth and recovery. The program focuses on addressing challenges such as addiction, unhealthy relationships, and personal accountability, while encouraging participants to pursue long-term positive change.

During opening remarks at the graduation, a long-term incarcerated participant who helped develop the program described its mission: “The Haven was created by incarcerated women for incarcerated women who struggle with habits, hangups, and who are working toward freedom from addiction, bondage, relationships, and finding liberty in Christ.”

The program is structured in three phases, with the first cohort completing Phase One: Refuge. Coursework during this phase includes instruction on emotional awareness, forgiveness, identity, recovery principles, life skills, codependency, and self-discovery. Participants live together in a shared unit, where they attend classes, share meals, and support one another through accountability and peer encouragement.

Dr. Beth Masters, chaplain and facilitator of The Haven program, emphasized the level of commitment required to complete the program. “You have chosen to work on yourself for a season, and that is what it takes. We have dug, and they have really examined themselves in this program. They have received certificates of completion for 11 in-person classes. They were also asked to complete a set of classes on their tablets. They have truly earned these certificates.”

Several participants were also recognized for reaching personal recovery milestones and received sobriety chips to mark their progress.

Graduate Whitney Hixson, an incarcerated individual who has recently been granted parole, shared her personal experience in the program, describing it as a turning point in her life. She noted that The Haven provided a structured, supportive environment where she could reflect, grow, and develop healthier coping strategies. Hixson also spoke about improvements in her relationships and her outlook on the future.

Program leaders emphasized that the initiative is designed to prepare participants for life both during incarceration and after release. “We are equipping women to live outside of this space, whether they are in their freedom outside of the gates or they return to our community,” the inmate facilitator said. “When they leave The Haven, they will carry what they have learned with them and share it with others.”

The program was launched with support from community partners, including First Baptist Church of Jackson, Crossgates Church of Brandon, and God Behind Bars.

MCIW Supt. Katrina Reid commended the graduates for their commitment to the program. “Recovery is a journey of a thousand steps, and today you took a significant one,” Reid said. “The tools you have learned can serve as a strong foundation for continued growth and progress.”

item.title: Retired Circuit Judge Robert Helfrich dies at age 72 - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
By Beverly Kraft Administrative Office of Courts

Retired Circuit Judge Robert Helfrich of Hattiesburg died on March 31 at Forrest General Hospital. He was 72.

Funeral arrangements are incomplete.

Judge Helfrich served as Circuit Judge of the 12th Circuit District of Forrest and Perry counties for more than 22 years. He officially retired on June 30, 2025, but continued to work without salary, presiding over the drug intervention court that he created shortly after he took office in 2003.

“He just really made a difference in the judicial system there, and he will be missed,” said retired Circuit Judge Jon Mark Weathers, who served alongside Judge Helfrich for more than eight years.

Judge Helfrich’s legacy includes working tirelessly to turn around the lives of drug addicts whom others had given up on, and righting wrongs committed to preserve segregation in the 1960s.

As an assistant district attorney for the 12th Circuit District, Helfrich reopened and prosecuted racially motivated crimes from the Civil Rights era. He headed the team that prosecuted Ku Klux Klan Imperial Wizard Samuel Bowers in 1998 for ordering the 1966 firebombing death of Vernon F. Dahmer Sr. Dahmer, a Civil Rights activist, successful businessman and farmer, had allowed Blacks to pay poll taxes at his store and had assisted with voter registration.

Hattiesburg attorney Pat Zachary, a longtime friend, said, “Bob was not afraid of anything. He would go back and try old civil rights cases that needed to be tried. He was straight up and brave about it.”

Circuit Judge Wes Curry of Hattiesburg, who came to the Circuit bench a year before Judge Helfrich retired, said, “I was in law school when he was assistant district attorney working on the Vernon Dahmer case, and it really made me proud that I came from a place that sought to do justice for the Dahmer family. He was a primary force in that case. To get to work with him and learn from him was very humbling.”

In 2006, as Circuit Judge, Helfrich ordered exoneration of Clyde Kennard, a Black man who was convicted of burglary involving receipt of stolen chicken feed in September 1960. Kennard had tried repeatedly to enroll in then all-white Mississippi Southern College. His defenders had long argued that Kennard was framed on the burglary charge to prevent him from pursuing college enrollment. He was diagnosed with cancer while serving a seven-year sentence at Parchman. He died in 1963, shortly after being released from prison. The man who testified against him recanted in 2005. After unsuccessful attempts to gain a gubernatorial pardon and Supreme Court vacation of the judgment, 16 people filed a Petition for Exoneration in Forrest County Circuit Court. On May 17, 2006, Judge Helfrich stated at a hearing that he was “compelled to do the right thing, and that is to declare Mr. Kennard innocent and to declare that the conviction of Mr. Kennard is hereby null and void.”

Weathers, who was District Attorney at the time, joined in the motion to exonerate on behalf of the State of Mississippi. Judge Helfrich “just did the right thing and wasn’t worried about the consequences,” he said.

Judge Helfrich was a leader in drug intervention courts. He was among the earliest to create separate tracks for veterans and DUI offenders within drug court. He was appointed in 2009 to the Board of Directors of the National Association of Drug Court Professionals, which later became known as All Rise. He served on the State Intervention Courts Advisory Committee for 12 years.

During his service on the NADCP Board of Directors, he introduced judges and court staff from across the country to some of his court’s innovations to keep participants involved in recovery. One of his early programs was basketball and softball teams for intervention court participants. He said in an interview, “It’s to show them there are things that you can do that are enjoyable that don’t involve the drug of choice.” And it was an opportunity for participants to receive encouragement. He cheered for them while serving as third base coach for the softball team when they played against other teams in Hattiesburg’s intramural league. Their canary yellow athletic shirts sported a “Helfrich’s Heroes” logo.

Judge Helfrich was passionate about saving those addicted to drugs. He accepted people into drug intervention court when others thought they were bound to fail. “He would want to try to save somebody and he thought he could do it,” Weathers said. He didn’t take just the first-time minor offenders. “He said, ‘I want the worst of the worst.’ He saved more of those than I ever thought that he would,” Weathers said.

Circuit Judge T. Michael Reed, who was appointed to the bench after Helfrich retired, said some of his own clients in private practice were accepted into drug intervention court when he didn’t think there was hope for them. “I would think this person is too far gone,” he recalled. Helfrich gave them a chance, and he held them accountable.

Colleagues recalled former intervention court participants who credited Helfrich for saving their lives. Zachary remembered one former intervention court participant who introduced himself at Fieldhouse for the Homeless, where Helfrich and fellow members of Parkway Heights United Methodist Church served breakfast every third Sunday. “He said, ‘You put me in jail because I didn’t mind what you told me in drug court. I needed to go and I don’t think I’d be alive today if it wasn’t for you.’”

Zachary said, “He loved his drug court participants and always wanted to do everything he could for them to keep them out of the prison system.”

Judge Curry said, “There are so many people who came through that drug court. They knew he cared about them and they loved him back…..He made the lives of those who came before him better.”

Weathers said, “It wasn’t just a job for him. It was a passion and it showed.”

He had a really gruff exterior, though.

Zachary recalled introducing Judge Helfrich a few years ago when Helfrich received the Hub Award, an annual honor recognizing individuals for exceptional public service and contributions to the community. Zachary had arranged to have Tootsie Pop candies on each table. “At the end, I compared him to a Tootsie Pop. Bob has a very gruff, tough exterior, but inside he was one of the warmest people and caring people for the underdog.”

The judge also loved dogs, keeping a canine companion with him in the courtroom. Stump, aptly named for his short legs, sat at the judge’s feet or napped on a mat under the bench during court, or slept on the couch in the judge’s office. After Stump passed away, Blaze took his place, accompanying the judge during court proceedings, ceremonies and work in his chambers.

Judge Helfrich was the son of Marjorie B. Helfrich, who was born in Ruleville, Mississippi, and Dutch military pilot Jan Eduard Helfrich. The couple met while both worked at Hawkins Field in Jackson during World War II. Marjorie Helfrich returned to Jackson to raise her six children after Jan Eduard Helfrich passed away.

Judge Helfrich served in the U.S. Coast Guard. He earned his undergraduate degree from George Mason University and his Juris Doctor from the University of Mississippi School of Law. He served as a public defender in Hattiesburg before becoming an assistant district attorney. He was elected to the 12th Circuit Court on Nov. 5, 2002, and took office on Jan. 1, 2003.

item.title: Pike County authorities seek public’s help regarding U-Haul seen on Magnolia Progress Road - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PIKE COUNTY – The Pike County Sheriff’s Office is asking for the public’s help regarding two individuals seen driving a U-Haul truck on Magnolia Progress Road.

In a community alert, the sheriff’s office asked anyone with information about the vehicle or who observed suspicious activity in the area to come forward.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Pike County Sheriff’s Office at 601-783-6767 or Crime Stoppers of Southwest Mississippi at 1-800-222-8477.

Officials did not release additional details about the individuals or the nature of the suspicious activity.

item.title: Paul B. Johnson State Park reopens after renovations, upgraded campsites and cabins - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
HATTIESBURG — Paul B. Johnson State Park has reopened following extensive renovations, with state officials highlighting upgraded campsites, cabins and amenities aimed at improving the visitor experience.

The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks marked the park’s grand reopening March 26 with a public event that included a morning social, a program featuring remarks from state Rep. Larry Byrd and tours of the updated facilities.

The park now features 129 renovated RV campsites equipped with full hookups, including water, electricity and sewer, along with picnic tables and grills.

In addition, officials said the park includes 12 newly renovated cabins and two duplexes. The cabins feature updated kitchens with stainless steel appliances, new dining areas, living room furniture with flatscreen televisions, and upgraded bedrooms and bathrooms with walk-in tile showers. The duplexes also include outdoor porches with picnic tables, fire pits and grills, as well as screened-in back porches with outdoor furniture.

Other improvements at the park include two bathhouses, a day-use restroom, a group camp bathhouse and new air conditioning units in multiple areas.

“The recent renovations at Paul B. Johnson State Park highlights our continued investment in Mississippi State Parks,” said MDWFP Executive Director Lynn Posey. “We are pleased to reopen the park and provide visitors with updated amenities and a chance to explore Mississippi’s great outdoors.”

Reservations for cabins and campsites are now open, according to the agency.

Visitors to the park can take part in activities including fishing, boating and use of a playground, nature trail and disc golf course. Admission is $2 per person, with free entry for children ages 5 and younger.

item.title: Mississippi Egg Marketing Board Hosts Easter at the Ag Museum - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Egg Marketing Board is hosting its annual Easter at the Ag Museum event on Saturday, April 4, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum.

“We’re proud to continue this annual Easter tradition at the Ag Museum and welcome visitors from all across the state,” said Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce Andy Gipson. “The Mississippi Egg Marketing Board does a wonderful job hosting this event each year and with the ‘Bunny Trail’ and hands-on activities to rides and family-friendly entertainment, there’s something for everyone to enjoy. It’s a great opportunity to spend time together and celebrate the season, and I encourage families to come out and be part of the festivities.”

Experience family-fun as children follow the tracks of the museum’s “Bunny Trail” to collect candy and toy-filled eggs in their baskets. Families will have the opportunity to dye and paint eggs; take a wagon, train or carousel ride; have their faces painted; and much more. This year, Mississippi’s Miss Hospitality Taylor Garretson and Miss Mississippi Anna Leah Jolly will be in attendance for a special meet and greet. The Mississippi Beef Council will also be serving complimentary hotdogs to visitors, while supplies last. Additional sponsors include Cal-Maine Foods and Polk’s Meat Products. Admission is $10 per person for ages 2 and up and includes carousel, train and wagon rides. Concessions will also be available for purchase.

The Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum, located at 1150 Lakeland Drive in Jackson, MS is open Monday through Saturday from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. For more information, call 601-432-4500, or visit the website www.msagmuseum.org or social media @msagmuseum. The Mississippi Agriculture and Forestry Museum is a division of Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce.

item.title: Man sentenced to 25 years attempted murder in DeSoto County stabbing - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HERNANDO – A man was sentenced to 25 years in prison after pleading guilty to attempted murder in connection with a stabbing at a construction site in Hernando, according to the DeSoto County District Attorney’s Office.

District Attorney Matthew Barton announced the conviction of Jiver Alejandro Melo Dominguez, a Mexican national who was living in Memphis at the time of the offense.

Authorities said the attack happened March 5, 2025, while Melo Dominguez and the victim were working at a construction site in Hernando. Investigators said Melo Dominguez stabbed his coworker, Jose Rene Artiga Pais, in the neck.

According to the district attorney’s office, Melo Dominguez later admitted he had planned to attack the victim that day because of ongoing personal issues between the two men.

Officials said Melo Dominguez was detained at the scene until law enforcement arrived.

Melo Dominguez pleaded guilty to attempted murder and was sentenced to 25 years in the custody of the Mississippi Department of Corrections, followed by 10 years of post-release supervision.

The case was investigated by the Hernando Police Department and prosecuted by Assistant District Attorney Ben Weathers.

In a statement, Barton commended the Hernando Police Department for its response and investigative work in the case.

item.title: Lauderdale County man charged with meth trafficking after traffic stop - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Greer Vari

item.title: Tyree Jones marks final day as Jackson police chief, thanks city and department leaders - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Hinds County Sheriff Tyree Jones said Tuesday was his final day serving as chief of the Jackson Police Department, bringing to a close a seven-month stretch in which he held both leadership roles.

In a statement, Jones said,

“Today is my final day serving as Chief of Police for the Jackson Police Department.” He added, “Leading this department during a critical transition period has been an honor, and I am grateful to Mayor John Horhn for his trust, confidence, and support over the past seven months.”

Jones said the experience was especially meaningful in the context of his long law enforcement career.

“Serving in the dual role of Hinds County Sheriff and Chief of Police has been one of the greatest highlights of my 26-year career, and I remain forever thankful for the opportunity,” he said.

He also thanked his family for their support during his time in the role.

“I want to thank my family for their unwavering support throughout this journey,” Jones said. “Their strength and encouragement have allowed me to serve our community with focus and commitment.”

Jones also praised officers and staff with both the Jackson Police Department and the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office.

“I am also deeply grateful to the men and women of both JPD and HCSO for their professionalism, dedication, and support in ensuring stability and continuity of operations in both departments,” he said. “Their service to our community is invaluable, and I am proud to stand with them.”

Jones said he remains optimistic about the city’s future and plans to continue working with Jackson leaders and public safety partners as sheriff.

“As a lifelong Jacksonian, I admire the progress our city continues to make, and it has been an honor to contribute to that progress,” he said. “In my ongoing role as Sheriff, I look forward to continuing strong partnerships with the City of Jackson, our community, and all public safety stakeholders.”

He also said he intends to support incoming Jackson Police Chief Dr. Rashell Brackney during the transition.

“I also look forward to supporting incoming Chief Dr. Rashell Brackney throughout this transition and as she assumes leadership of the department,” Jones said.

Jones closed his statement by thanking the city directly.

“Thank you, Jackson, for your support and for the privilege to serve,” he said. “Jackson Rising.”

item.title: Jackson Mayor Urges Residents to Apply for Tornado Recovery Program Before Deadline - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Mayor John Horhn is urging eligible homeowners to apply for a state-administered recovery program before a fast-approaching deadline to receive assistance for storm-damaged homes.

The Mississippi Homeowner Rehabilitation & Reconstruction Program, administered by the Mississippi Development Authority, provides federally funded aid to low- and moderate-income homeowners whose homes were damaged or destroyed during the April 8-11, 2024, tornadoes and straight-line winds.

Applications are due by 11:59 p.m. Sunday, April 5, 2026.

“Many Jackson families are still working to recover from these devastating storms, and this program can provide critical help to rebuild what was lost,” Horhn said in a statement. “I encourage every eligible homeowner to apply before the deadline and take advantage of this opportunity for support.”

According to the Mississippi Housing Recovery program, applicants must have unrepaired storm damage, own and occupy the home as their primary residence and meet income requirements at or below 80% of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development’s area median income. Eligible properties include those located in Hinds County.

Homeowners can apply online, by phone or in person through the Mississippi Housing Recovery website. Applicants should be prepared to provide documentation including proof of identity, income, homeownership, residency, insurance coverage and any disaster assistance previously received.

For Jackson-area residents seeking in-person help, an intake center is available at the Edwards Community Center in Edwards. There is no cost to apply or participate in the program.

More information is available at mshousingrecovery.com or by calling 866-981-7727.

item.title: MISSING IN MISSISSIPPI: Frank Garcia, Chickasaw County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
CHICKASAW COUNTY — A Houston man who walked away from his home carrying his belongings in February 1994 has never been found, and investigators are still seeking information that could help solve his disappearance.

Frank Garcia, a 35-year-old Hispanic man, was last seen on Feb. 16, 1994, walking away from his residence on Highway 8 East in Houston. He was carrying two garbage bags of clothes, a 19-inch television and a box of important papers at the time.

Garcia was not reported missing until nearly a week later, when he failed to pick up two paychecks from his employer and no one had heard from him.

He is described as 5 feet, 5 inches tall, weighing approximately 140 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Garcia has tattoos reading “Nancy” on one arm and “Ginger” on the other.

The case is being investigated by the Mississippi Department of Public Safety and the Chickasaw County Sheriff’s Department. Garcia remains missing as of the publication of this report.

Anyone with information on Garcia’s whereabouts is asked to contact the Mississippi Department of Public Safety at (662) 563-6400 or the Chickasaw County Sheriff’s Department at (662) 456-3513.

item.title: Lary Aaron to headline Legacy League Hot Stove event April 3 in Jackson - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Lary Aaron, son of baseball legend Hank Aaron, will make a special guest appearance April 3 at a Hot Stove event in Jackson to support the inaugural season of the Legacy League, organizers announced.

item.title: Hinds County murder suspect arrested after two-vehicle crash in Jones County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HINDS COUNTY – A 19-year-old man wanted on a capital murder warrant out of Hinds County was arrested Sunday night after deputies responded to a two-vehicle crash in Jones County.

Jackson teen arrested on capital murder charges

Deputies Kalob Broadway and Will Ladd responded to the scene and, during the crash investigation, determined that one of the vehicle’s occupants, Zachary Stevens, was listed in the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database as wanted by the Hinds County Sheriff’s Office on a capital murder warrant.

Stevens was arrested at the scene and taken to the Jones County Adult Detention Facility, where he is being held pending extradition to Hinds County.

item.title: Five killed, one injured in train-van crash in Stone County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
STONE COUNTY – Five people were killed and a sixth was seriously injured Friday afternoon when a train collided with a van in Stone County, according to WLOX.

Stone County Sheriff Todd Stewart told WLOX the crash happened around 1 p.m. at Pump Branch Road, just off Highway 49. First responders had to cut their way through the woods to reach the wreckage, the station reported.

Authorities said six people were inside the van at the time of the crash. Stone County Coroner Wayne Flurry confirmed that five of them died at the scene, and the sixth person was airlifted to a hospital in New Orleans.

WLOX later reported the five people killed were identified as 26-year-old Ryan C. Peterson, 23-year-old Demarcus Perkins, 45-year-old Kristina Carver, and Carver’s two daughters, 22-year-old Emley Chamblee and 20-year-old Sarabeth Chamblee.

The station also reported that the railroad crossing at Pump Branch Road does not have crossing arms or lights. Stone County District 1 Supervisor Jimmy Springs told WLOX that crossarms are planned for the crossing, but installation could take up to a year.

item.title: Eight families displaced after apartment fire on West Capitol Street in Jackson - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Eight families were displaced Sunday morning after a fire damaged multiple units at an apartment complex on West Capitol Street, according to the Jackson Fire Department.

Firefighters were called at 8:49 a.m. Sunday to 1315 W. Capitol St., the Magnolia Apartments, for a reported structure fire.

When crews arrived, they found smoke and flames coming from the building, officials said.

After the fire was extinguished, the origin and cause could not immediately be determined, and a fire investigator was called to the scene.

Investigators later classified the cause of the fire as undetermined, according to the fire department. Officials said the investigation remains ongoing as additional information becomes available.

The fire damaged eight apartment units and displaced eight families, authorities said. The American Red Cross is assisting those affected.

No injuries were reported.

item.title: Casino burglary suspect caught by Tunica County K-9 after lengthy chase - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUNICA COUNTY – A Tunica man was arrested Friday night after authorities said he was linked to a vehicle burglary at a Robinsonville casino, then led deputies on a chase that ended in a crash and foot pursuit.

The Tunica County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were called around 9:14 p.m. Friday to a casino in Robinsonville after receiving a report of a vehicle burglary in the parking lot.

Witnesses provided a description of the suspects’ vehicle, and that information was broadcast to patrol deputies, according to the sheriff’s office.

At about 9:52 p.m., a deputy spotted a vehicle matching the description near Old Highway 61 and Casino Strip Drive and attempted a traffic stop. Authorities said the driver refused to stop, leading deputies on a high-speed chase before losing control of the vehicle and fleeing on foot.

Deputies then pursued the suspect on foot and used a sheriff’s office K-9 to make the arrest, officials said.

Authorities identified the suspect as Deonte Taylor, 20, of Tunica. Taylor suffered a dog bite during the apprehension and was treated at an area hospital before being taken to the Tunica County Jail.

Taylor was charged with failure to stop, possession of a stolen firearm, possession of burglary tools, conspiracy, burglary of a vehicle and felony fleeing.

The sheriff’s office said Taylor had also been out on bond in connection with a 2023 triple homicide case in Tunica County, where he faced capital murder and other charges.

Officials said Taylor was given a $45,000 bond on the new charges.

The investigation remains ongoing. Anyone with information is asked to contact CrimeStoppers at 662-910-0400 or the Tunica County Sheriff’s Office at 662-363-1411.

item.title: Attala County manhunt ends with suspect dead - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
ATTALA COUNTY – A man wanted in connection with a shooting that left two people dead in Attala County is now dead, according to the sheriff’s department. Attala County Sheriff Curtis Pope posted on Facebook early Monday that the suspect was killed while trying to enter someone’s home.

The suspect was identified as Christopher Hughes. Before his death, Carthage police had described him as armed and dangerous in connection with the Sunday shootings. The identities of the two victims had not been released as of Monday morning.

In response to the situation, the Kosciusko School District canceled three bus routes Monday for student safety. Those routes were 65-03, known as Culpepper, 81-14, known as Jamison, and 78-12, known as Ford. School officials asked parents who could transport their children to do so and said anyone unable to bring students to school should contact the school office.

Breezy News also reported that two additional routes, those of Mrs. Collins and Mrs. Veasley, would not run Monday.

School officials said the safety of students and staff remained their top priority.

item.title: Opera Mississippi to Perform 'Songs for a New World' in Jackson - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Opera Mississippi will bring Tony Award-winning composer Jason Robert Brown’s “Songs for a New World” to Duling Hall in Jackson on April 24-25, offering audiences two nights of professional musical theatre centered on themes of change, resilience and hope.

Tickets are $35 per person. Each evening begins with an Opera Happy Hour at 6 p.m., with the concert starting at 7 p.m. Duling Hall is located at 622 Duling Ave.

The production features four professional vocalists: John Christopher Adams, Maryann Kyle, Peter Lake and Sarah Stembel. They will be performing a song cycle that blends pop, gospel and contemporary musical theatre. Rather than a traditional narrative, the show presents a series of self-contained scenes depicting people at pivotal moments of transformation.

Brown, who won a Tony Award for “The Bridges of Madison County,” wrote “Songs for a New World” as his debut stage work. The piece has since become a staple of regional and professional musical theatre nationally.

Founded in 1945, Opera Mississippi is the ninth oldest continuously operating opera company in the United States and the state’s only professional opera company. The organization’s mission includes educational outreach, emerging artist development and preserving the operatic art form.

Tickets are available at operamississippi.org .

item.title: Mississippi Man, 83, Charged After Striking Firefighter With Vehicle - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON COUNTY — An 83-year-old Jackson County man is facing a felony charge after allegedly striking a U.S. Forest Service firefighter with his vehicle while attempting to bypass a road closure during an active forest fire Saturday evening.

Tommy Broadnax was charged with simple assault on a firefighter following the approximately 5:45 p.m. incident on Stephen Earl Drive in the Latimer Community, according to Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter.

Firefighters and U.S. Forest Service personnel had closed the roadway while working to contain a forest fire in the area. When Broadnax was told the road was closed, authorities said he became agitated and refused to comply with orders from first responders. A Forest Service firefighter attempted to stop him and repeat the warning, but Broadnax struck her with his vehicle, knocking her to the ground, before continuing down the road.

Broadnax was taken into custody without further incident. Under Mississippi law, simple assault on a firefighter is a felony offense.

The Jackson County Sheriff’s Office is asking anyone with additional information to contact the agency at (228) 769-3063.
